scenarios.title: Automated video editing agents delete master footage when cleanup permissions lack safeguards
scenarios.world: It is 2029. Commercial media studios, newsrooms, and design firms routinely employ autonomous software agents to ingest footage, synchronize multicam audio, grade color profiles, and clear intermediate render scratch caches overnight. Most post-production houses connect their editing suites to enterprise cloud storage where agents hold broad read, write, and delete permissions to manage disk quotas. Editors arrive in the morning expecting finalized timeline exports, but frequently encounter wiped project directories when an agent's recursive cleanup script misinterprets relative symlinks or project hierarchy tags. Small independent production houses that rely on unmanaged automated agents suffer complete project losses, while larger conglomerates mandate centralized proprietary cloud locks that prevent independent editors from controlling their own local assets.
scenarios.premise: Broadcaster incidents and community audits reveal that autonomous production agents with ambient file deletion privileges delete finished series footage and staging directories during automated cleanup tasks. When agents treat primary filesystems as scratch spaces without immutable snapshots or two-party authorization, software bugs cause catastrophic data destruction that standard backups fail to prevent.
scenarios.how: The collective intelligence network demonstrates that local containment and fractured authority protect creative data without surrender to centralized cloud monopolies. By specifying host-level runtime contracts where personal agents operate strictly within isolated virtual sandboxes, tools receive temporary scratch spaces while master storage remains read-only. Destructive file operations require cryptographic authorization from the person's own private device, providing resilience against automated deletion bugs without cloud surveillance.

outcomes.name: Unconstrained agents cause permanent data destruction across production studios
outcomes.description: Production firms and design studios grant agents direct file management access, leading to catastrophic asset deletions when automated tasks mistake production masters for temporary render caches.
outcomes.example: An independent documentary studio in Stockholm loses six months of color-graded 4K master files when their automated archival agent misidentifies the primary volume as an expired proxy folder.

outcomes.name: Immutable copy-on-write storage and two-person authorization become standard
outcomes.description: Creative tooling adopts append-only local storage engines and host-mediated authorization barriers where no agent can perform irreversible deletions without explicit human sign-off.
outcomes.example: A podcast network runs fifty audio processing agents across their network, with host storage drivers that enforce immutable file versions and require signed user confirmations before any disk space reclamation.

outcomes.name: Proprietary cloud platforms enforce vendor lock-in under safety justifications
outcomes.description: Major cloud vendors use data loss incidents to mandate that all media editing occur inside proprietary walled gardens, stripping creators of direct local file access.
outcomes.example: A global streaming service requires all subcontracted video editors to use browser-streamed virtual workstations that forbid local file storage or self-hosted agent automation.

scenarios.title: Automated vulnerability hunters outrun software patchers and trigger runaway security backlogs
scenarios.world: It is 2029. Automated auditing agents continuously scan open-source packages, corporate repositories, and device firmware, uncovering hundreds of zero-day vulnerabilities every day. Software engineering teams and independent maintainers are flooded with automated bug reports and machine-generated patches. Because every patch must be vetted to prevent regressions or supply chain tampering, defensive triage cannot keep pace with offensive generation. Critical infrastructure operators, healthcare providers, and consumer devices run with known unpatched exploits for weeks at a time. Attack scripts automatically branch and mutate across systems, while defenders rely on fragile prioritization algorithms that fail when attacker populations surge.
scenarios.premise: Recent mathematical modeling of dynamic attack surfaces shows that accelerating offensive vulnerability discovery alongside defensive patching does not preserve security parity. When autonomous agents discover flaws faster than systems can test and deploy safe updates, software transitions into an unbounded-risk state where backlogs of live exploits grow indefinitely.
scenarios.how: The network develops personal twin runtimes and agent contracts built on structural capability containment and local memory isolation. Rather than relying on faster patching races, the network designs systems where individual agents operate with minimal ambient authority and explicit data flow boundaries, reducing the blast radius of unpatched vulnerabilities.

outcomes.name: Defenders fall into an unbounded exploit backlog
outcomes.description: The pace of agentic vulnerability discovery permanently outstrips defensive review capacity, causing exploit windows to expand and making public software indefinitely vulnerable.
outcomes.example: A municipal water district delays patching three automated zero-day notices for 45 days due to maintainer overload, during which time automated botnets compromise its telemetry systems.

outcomes.name: Deterministic containment architectures reduce reliance on frantic patching
outcomes.description: Systems adopt strict memory and capability boundaries that prevent untrusted code execution and confine compromised components, keeping systems safe even when known flaws remain unpatched.
outcomes.example: A hospital network isolates its diagnostic assistants within capability-bounded runtime containers; an unpatched parser vulnerability is exploited by a botnet but fails to gain network egress or read patient records.
